endorsements.quote: Periodic sample-based clinician review: Qualified, independent clinician adjudicators review samples of real-world inputs and outputs against prospectively defined criteria, sampled to reflect the range of clinically relevant presentations and interaction patterns the device encounters in real-world use.

endorsements.quote: Re-evaluation of AI model performance using updated local data sets at specified intervals, but at least annually, may be an appropriate monitoring mechanism for models where gathering real-time data on model performance is limited (quantification, workflow enhancement, etc.) or in instances where patient safety will not be immediately impacted ( 80 ).

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Algorithms in Health Care: Is the Current Food and Drug Administration Regulation Sufficient?

endorsements.title: Achieving Equity in Generative Artificial Intelligence in Cardiovascular Medicine

endorsements.title: A testable framework linking diagnostic AI contribution to outcome measurement in clinical decision support

evidence.title: Standardised evaluation and monitoring of site-specific AI performance with physical CT phantoms
evidence.effect: Longitudinal monitoring of AI performance using the physical phantoms yielded consistent results over a 15-month period across two systems.
evidence.quote: Next, we perform longitudinal monitoring, yielding consistent results over fifteen months on both systems.

evidence.title: Importance of model governance in clinical AI models: case study on the relevance of data drift detection
evidence.outcome: Monthly AUC monitoring against limits from cross-validation performance
evidence.effect: Temporal validation AUC 0.82 and Brier 0.158; monthly AUC dipped below the 3 SD limit twice (March 2020, March 2021), otherwise within limits.
evidence.quote: The AUC dipped slightly below our performance limit on two occasions: in March 2020 and March 2021.

evidence.title: Detecting changes in the performance of a clinical machine learning tool over time
evidence.outcome: Predictive performance relative to original validation
evidence.effect: Follow-up AUC was 0.78 versus original validation AUCs between 0.75 and 0.81; AUPRC was 0.41 versus previous AUPRCs between 0.19 and 0.38.
evidence.quote: The average AUC (0.78) during this follow-up is comparable to the original validations (AUCs ranging between 0.75 and 0.81), while the AUPRC (0.41) even is slightly higher (previous AUPRCs ranging between 0.19 and 0.38).

evidence.title: An analysis of the real world performance of an artificial intelligence based autism diagnostic
evidence.outcome: Real-world diagnostic performance compared with original clinical trial performance
evidence.effect: Clinical trial versus real world: PPV 80.8% versus 92.4% (p=0.024); NPV 98.2% versus 97.6% (p=1.0); determinate rate 31.8% versus 63.0% (p<0.001).
evidence.quote: Compared to clinical trial results, real world performance was equivalent for all key metrics, with the exception of the determinate rate and the PPV which were significantly improved in real world performance.

evidence.title: Performance Drift in a Nationally Deployed Population Health Risk Algorithm in the US Veterans Health Administration
evidence.outcome: Loss of accuracy relative to initial performance in a deployed national model
evidence.effect: Performance declined 2016-2021 from shifts in outcome prevalence and covariates: PPV fell 4.0%, F1 fell 4.6%, FPR rose; event rate fell from 3.8% (2017) to 3.0% (2021).
evidence.quote: This cohort study found that CAN algorithm performance declined from 2016 to 2021 due to shifts in outcome prevalence and distributions of health care utilization and demographic covariates.

evidence.title: Validation is not enough: Longitudinal evidence of post-deployment fragility in clinical AI systems
evidence.effect: validation-era performance deteriorated post-deployment across all 4 evaluated AI systems
evidence.quote: Across all systems, validation-era performance did not persist as a stable operational property after deployment.
evidence.sample_unit: deployed AI systems (1,814,000 inference events total)

evidence.title: Standardised evaluation and monitoring of site-specific AI performance with physical CT phantoms
evidence.outcome: Longitudinal AI performance stability on physical phantoms
evidence.effect: Longitudinal monitoring yielded consistent results over fifteen months on both systems.
evidence.quote: Next, we perform longitudinal monitoring, yielding consistent results over fifteen months on both systems.

evidence.title: Silent calibration drift in a frozen clinical prediction model: a decade-long audit and an operational monitoring framework
evidence.outcome: Loss of calibration relative to original validation over a decade of static deployment
evidence.effect: Discrimination stable, but calibration intercept drifted (-0.54, -0.31) with over-prediction as baseline mortality fell from 20.5% to 15.6%.
evidence.quote: Discrimination-based validation can conceal clinically meaningful calibration drift.

evidence.title: Temporal External Validation of Successive RCRI (Revised Cardiac Risk Index) Updates across Observational Healthcare Databases: a Multinational Retrospective Cohort Study
evidence.outcome: AUROC of RCRI versions across 6-month intervals from 2010 to 2025
evidence.effect: AUROC showed a statistically significant decrease (p = 0.0099) over time across eight databases; calibration and Net-Benefit relatively consistent.
evidence.quote: The Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve showed a statistically significant (p = 0.0099) decrease.

evidence.title: Performance drift is a major barrier to the safe use of machine learning in cardiac surgery
evidence.outcome: Loss of model accuracy over time relative to initial validation
evidence.effect: Performance of ML and ES II declined over time after temporal split; ML remained superior to ES II; regular assessment and modification suggested.
evidence.quote: ML performance decreases over time due to dataset drift, but remains superior to ES II.

evidence.title: Performance Drift in Machine Learning Models for Cardiac Surgery Risk Prediction: Retrospective Analysis
evidence.outcome: Loss of accuracy relative to initial validation over time in temporally split holdout
evidence.effect: All models showed decreased CEM, AUC, and F1 over the 2017-2019 holdout; XGBoost AUC slope -0.000678; NN net benefit fell from 0.9035 to 0.8808 in projection.
evidence.quote: We found strong evidence that all models showed a decrease in at least 3 of the 5 individual metrics within the CEM.

commentary.bottom_line: Two small offline studies suggest that scheduled re-evaluation against a fixed local reference can run for 15 months and can flag months when performance falls outside preset limits, but no study shows that the practice prevents harm to patients. Six of nine hazard reports found loss of accuracy or calibration after initial validation, and two of those six draw on the same UK cardiac surgery cohort.

perspectives.view: Two studies test the practice, both at evidence level 4 in offline or simulated settings. One followed two CT systems with physical phantoms for 15 months, and the other monitored monthly AUC in 6,822 Dutch admissions. Neither compared re-evaluation with no re-evaluation or measured patient outcomes, so certainty is very low because of indirectness and imprecision.

A lung-resection model was used unchanged for a decade. Its discrimination held steady, while the calibration intercept drifted to between -0.54 and -0.31, with over-prediction as baseline mortality fell from 20.5% to 15.6%. The Dutch monitoring study tracked AUC alone. A schedule limited to discrimination may therefore miss calibration loss that changes individual risk estimates.

In the Dutch study, monthly AUC fell below a 3 SD limit set from cross-validation twice, in March 2020 and March 2021, and otherwise stayed within limits. The phantom study found stable results over 15 months on two CT systems. This suggests the method is workable in practice, but its ability to detect real decline remains untested.

Neither test of the practice reported the payer, language, or literacy characteristics of patients, and the monitoring study was conducted in the Netherlands. The largest hazard study covered 7,215,711 veterans, a population that differs from Medicaid and safety-net patients. This evidence does not measure how performance changes over time within subgroups.

The supplied sources recommend periodic re-evaluation but do not require it. The radiology multi-society statement proposes re-evaluation on updated local data at least annually. CHAI gives quarterly review as an example cadence, and a regulator discussion paper describes periodic clinician review of samples. The quoted Utah statute addresses disclosure of AI use, not performance re-evaluation.

Two real deployments found no loss. In one, AUC was 0.78 against original values between 0.75 and 0.81. In the other, PPV rose from 80.8% to 92.4%. This suggests decline is not uniform, so risk-tiered schedules like those RUAIH describes may help direct effort. No study reported the staff time or cost of maintaining local evaluation datasets.

A national VA model covered 7,215,711 veterans. From 2016 to 2021, its PPV fell 4.0% and its F1 score fell 4.6%, as the event rate dropped from 3.8% to 3.0%. No study reported whether re-evaluation findings reached patients or clinicians, or whether they changed the care patients received.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared scheduled re-evaluation with no re-evaluation in a live deployment. No study measured whether detected declines led to model updates or fewer patient harms, and none tested how often re-evaluation should occur. Studies that track calibration and subgroup performance alongside discrimination, and that report the cost of maintaining local evaluation datasets, would address the main uncertainties.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither study testing the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot tell from this evidence whether scheduled re-evaluation would detect declines that affect their patients. They may need to include such patients deliberately in their local evaluation datasets.
